scenes.head: Working capital and capital spending
scenes.sub: EBITDA is not cash. Two schedules explain most of the gap: working capital, the cash tied up in customers who have not paid and stock not yet sold, and capital spending, the cash that buys the equipment depreciation later spreads over the years. Build both for Lantern.

segs.say: Working capital and capital spending. EBITDA is not cash. Two schedules explain most of the gap: working capital, the cash tied up in customers who have not paid and stock not yet sold, and capital spending, the cash that buys the equipment depreciation later spreads over the years. Build both for Lantern.

scenes.head: You will be able to

segs.say: Forecast receivables, inventory, payables and other working capital balances from days and shares, each measured against the right driver.
Calculate the change in working capital and explain its effect on cash.
Build a fixed asset schedule: capital spending, depreciation by asset from the month it comes into use, and the roll-forward of property and equipment.
Evaluate capital spending against depreciation, asset lives and the business’s plans.
Explain why the model’s book depreciation and the tax depreciation used in F05 differ, and what the model leaves out.

scenes.head: Ana’s forecast shows EBITDA of $23,319 in 2028.

segs.say: Ana’s forecast shows EBITDA of $23,319 in 2028. Coastline’s credit officer is more interested in cash, because loans are repaid in cash, and in 2028 Lantern will spend $105,000 on the second kitchen and Cold Brew’s fridges, collect a large payment owed at the end of 2027, and carry more stock and more customer invoices as it grows. None of that is in EBITDA. This lesson builds the two schedules that turn profit into cash.

scenes.head: A business that sells on credit records revenue when it delivers, but collects the cash later; until then, the money sits in receivables.

segs.say: A business that sells on credit records revenue when it delivers, but collects the cash later; until then, the money sits in receivables. It buys stock before selling it, so cash sits in inventory. On the other side, it buys from suppliers on credit, so their money sits in payables, and some customers pay in advance, so theirs sits in unearned revenue. The difference is operating working capital: the cash the business has tied up in its day-to-day operations. When working capital grows, cash is used; when it shrinks, cash is released, even if profit is unchanged.

scenes.head: Growth is the usual cause.

segs.say: Growth is the usual cause. If Lantern’s catering doubles, so do the invoices waiting to be paid at any moment. That is why fast-growing businesses can be profitable and still run short of cash, the problem F00 and F05 both warned about, and why a lender wants to see working capital forecast line by line rather than ignored.

scenes.head: Each balance is forecast from the flow it comes from, measured in days.

segs.say: Each balance is forecast from the flow it comes from, measured in days. Days sales outstanding says how many days of credit sales are waiting to be collected; days inventory outstanding, how many days of cost of goods sit in stock; days payables outstanding, how many days of purchases are owed to suppliers. F03 measured them on Lantern’s 2027 accounts. Ana rounds them into assumptions:
Lantern’s working capital drivers

scenes.head: The balance at each year end is the flow for the year times the days, divided by 365.

segs.say: The balance at each year end is the flow for the year times the days, divided by 365. For 2028: invoiced revenue of $283,578 at 25 days gives receivables of $19,423; Cold Brew’s $64,914 at 60 days adds $10,671; together $30,094, nearly three times 2027’s $10,698. Inventory and payables both come to $12,330 because both are 21 days of the same cost of goods.

scenes.head: The working capital schedule

segs.say: Lantern’s working capital, 31 December each year (dollars)

scenes.head: Working capital falls by $15,219 in 2028, releasing cash, although receivables nearly triple.

segs.say: Working capital falls by $15,219 in 2028, releasing cash, although receivables nearly triple. The reason is the one-off: the $30,840 contract asset, revenue Lantern earned in 2027 under a year’s catering contract with a law firm that pays in one sum at the end of the contract year, is collected when the firm pays on 31 March 2028. Without it working capital would have risen. From 2029 the schedule settles into a pattern: a rise of $6,216 in 2029 as sales grow, then small changes as growth slows. A lender reads 2028’s release with care: it is real cash, but it will not happen again.

scenes.head: The sign that trips everyone

segs.say: The sign that trips everyone. An increase in a working capital asset (receivables, inventory) uses cash; an increase in a working capital liability (payables, unearned revenue) provides cash. In the cash flow statement, the change in operating working capital is subtracted from profit: a positive change means cash went into the business.

chapters.title: Choosing the right driver for each balance

scenes.head: Most errors in working capital forecasts come from measuring a balance against the wrong flow.

segs.say: Most errors in working capital forecasts come from measuring a balance against the wrong flow. Receivables come only from sales customers have not paid for yet, so they are measured against invoiced revenue: catering, training and the second kitchen’s wholesale bakery, and Cold Brew separately because grocers take longer to pay. Measuring them against total revenue would dilute the days with card sales that are never owed, and the forecast would go wrong as soon as the mix changed. Inventory and payables are measured against cost of goods sold, because stock is carried at cost and suppliers are paid at cost. Wages payable follow the wage bill, unearned revenue the revenue that customers pay for in advance (training places, subscriptions, catering deposits), and taxes payable the year’s tax charge.

scenes.head: Year-end balances can also mislead in a seasonal business.

segs.say: Year-end balances can also mislead in a seasonal business. If Lantern’s catering peaked every December, its receivables at 31 December would be higher than in a typical month, and days measured at the year end would overstate the cash tied up during most of the year. A monthly model would catch that; an annual model can only use year-end balances consistently and note the risk. Lantern’s year-end is not unusually busy, so year-end days are a fair measure.

chapters.title: From days to the cash conversion cycle

scenes.head: The three days measures combine into the cash conversion cycle: days of inventory plus days of receivables minus days of payables.

segs.say: The three days measures combine into the cash conversion cycle: days of inventory plus days of receivables minus days of payables. It is roughly how long a dollar spent on stock takes to come back as cash from a customer. For Lantern the measure needs care, because its receivables and its inventory belong to different lines (invoiced customers against goods sold in the cafés and online), so a single cycle for the whole business mixes unlike things. In a model it is more useful line by line, and as a check on the assumptions: a forecast whose cycle shortens sharply, without new payment terms or a change in how stock is bought, is manufacturing cash on paper.

scenes.head: Some balances at the start of a forecast will not recur and should not be grown with sales.

segs.say: Some balances at the start of a forecast will not recur and should not be grown with sales. Lantern’s contract asset is one: nine months of a year’s catering for a law firm, recognised as Lantern delivered it in 2027, but paid in one sum of $41,120 only when the contract year ends on 31 March 2028. No contract on those terms is planned again. The model therefore takes the balance to zero in 2028 instead of forecasting it in days. Other common examples are a large customer deposit received just before the year end, a tax refund due, or a one-time prepayment. Each needs its own line, run off on its own timetable, and a note saying why.

scenes.head: Most working capital lines are also current assets and current liabilities, so they feed straight into Coastline’s covenant, the current ratio of at…

segs.say: Most working capital lines are also current assets and current liabilities, so they feed straight into Coastline’s covenant, the current ratio of at least 1.2. That ties the working capital assumptions to the bank’s question in ways that are easy to miss. Faster collection lowers receivables and raises cash by the same amount, leaving current assets unchanged; but if the cash is then used to repay the line of credit, current liabilities fall too and the ratio improves. Paying suppliers more slowly raises payables, a current liability, and so lowers the ratio, even though it helps cash. Unearned revenue does the same: customers paying in advance is good for cash and bad for the current ratio. A model built with each balance on its own line lets Ana see these effects before Coastline does, and lesson 6 tests the covenant year by year once the statements are linked.

scenes.head: Capital spending is the cash paid for long-lived assets; depreciation spreads their cost over the years they are used.

segs.say: Capital spending is the cash paid for long-lived assets; depreciation spreads their cost over the years they are used. The model keeps them in a fixed asset schedule: one row per asset or group, its cost, the month it comes into use, its monthly depreciation and its life, and below them the totals for each year. Lantern’s schedule has the five groups of assets it owned at the end of 2027 (F02 and F03), the three it buys in 2028 (F05), and Ana’s allowance for replacements.
Depreciation in 2028, asset by asset (dollars)

scenes.head: The assets bought in April 2028 are depreciated for nine months that year: the kitchen’s equipment, 60,000 ÷ 84 × 9 = 6,429 dollars.

segs.say: The assets bought in April 2028 are depreciated for nine months that year: the kitchen’s equipment, 60,000 ÷ 84 × 9 = 6,429 dollars. Property and equipment then roll forward: the net book value at the start of the year, plus capital spending, less depreciation, gives the net book value at the end. For 2028: 95,400 + 105,000 − 35,979 = 164,421.

scenes.head: Three checks catch most capital spending errors.

segs.say: Three checks catch most capital spending errors. First, compare it with depreciation over several years: a business that spends far less than its depreciation is letting its assets run down, and its forecast margins will not last. Ana’s first draft allowed $10,000 a year for replacements against depreciation of over $40,000; she raised it to $25,000 a year from 2029. Second, look at asset lives: Lantern’s café fit-out and espresso machines are fully depreciated by early 2032, when the café leases come up for renewal, so the model adds a refit of $54,000 in March 2032. Third, ask whether the plan needs assets the schedule leaves out: a third kitchen, more delivery vans. Capital spending of $105,000 in 2028, $25,000 a year from 2029 and $79,000 in 2032 is lumpy, as real capital spending is.

chapters.title: Book depreciation, tax depreciation and leases

scenes.head: The model depreciates every asset straight line, for its accounts and for its tax, which is a simplification.

segs.say: The model depreciates every asset straight line, for its accounts and for its tax, which is a simplification. F05 used the US tax system’s MACRS schedules, which deduct more in the early years; the difference would create a deferred tax liability on Lantern’s balance sheet. For a small model the effect is small and is left out, and the lessons say so. The cafés’ leases are kept as a right-of-use asset and an equal lease liability that run down together, because their payments are level; their cost stays in occupancy, as in 2027. The second kitchen’s rent is treated as an expense when paid, another stated simplification.

scenes.head: A working capital balance from days

segs.say: A working capital balance from days: Balanceₜ = Flowₜ × Days/365.
Flowₜ: The revenue or cost the balance comes from, for year t (invoiced revenue for receivables, cost of goods for inventory and payables) ($).
Days: The assumed days outstanding (days).
It assumes this: The year-end balance reflects an average year; seasonal businesses may need a different measure.

scenes.head: Change in operating working capital

segs.say: Change in operating working capital: ΔNWCₜ = NWCₜ − NWCₜ₋₁.
NWCₜ: Operating current assets minus operating current liabilities at the end of year t ($).
It assumes this: Cash, debt and interest payable are excluded: they belong to financing.
A positive change uses cash; it is subtracted from profit in the cash flow statement.

scenes.head: Roll-forward of property and equipment

segs.say: Roll-forward of property and equipment: NBVₜ = NBVₜ₋₁ + Capexₜ − Depreciationₜ.
NBVₜ: Net book value (cost less accumulated depreciation) at the end of year t ($).
Capexₜ: Capital spending in year t ($).
It assumes this: No disposals; a sale would also remove the asset’s book value.

scenes.head: Straight-line depreciation by month

segs.say: Straight-line depreciation by month: D_y = (Cost − Residual)/(Life in months) × Months in use in year y.
D_y: Depreciation in calendar year y ($).
Months in use in year y: From the month it comes into use, until the life ends (months).
It assumes this: Straight line; the asset is used evenly over its life.

chapters.title: Example: Receivables at the end of 2028

scenes.head: Receivables at the end of 2028

segs.say: In 2028 the model forecasts catering revenue of $124,278, training of $46,800, second-kitchen revenue of $112,500 and Cold Brew revenue of $64,914. Customers who are invoiced take 25 days to pay; grocers take 60 days. Café and online sales are paid at once. Forecast receivables at 31 December 2028.

scenes.head: Receivables at the end of 2028

segs.say: Step 3. Cold Brew at 60 days: 64,914 × 60 ÷ 365 = 10,671.

scenes.head: Receivables at the end of 2028

segs.say: About $30,094 of receivables, against $10,698 a year earlier.
The kitchen’s wholesale and catering invoices, and the grocers’ 60-day terms, tie up about $19,400 more of Lantern’s cash than at the end of 2027.

chapters.title: Example: Why working capital releases cash in 2028

scenes.head: Why working capital releases cash in 2028

segs.say: Operating working capital was $26,956 at the end of 2027 and is forecast at $11,737 at the end of 2028. Explain the change from its parts.

scenes.head: Why working capital releases cash in 2028

segs.say: Step 1. Assets: receivables rise 19,396, inventory 2,855; the contract asset falls 30,840 when the law firm pays; prepaid is unchanged. Net change in assets: -8,589.
Step 2. Liabilities: payables rise 3,050, wages payable 1,969, unearned revenue 4,588; income taxes payable fall 2,977 to zero, because 2028 is a loss year. Net change in liabilities: 6,630.
Step 3. Change in working capital = change in assets − change in liabilities = -15,219: a fall, so it releases 15,219 of cash.
Step 4. Without the contract asset, working capital would have risen by 15,621, using cash.

scenes.head: Why working capital releases cash in 2028

segs.say: Working capital falls by $15,219: the $30,840 collected from the law firm outweighs the growth in receivables and inventory.
A one-off release flatters 2028’s cash. Coastline will discount it when judging whether Lantern’s operations generate cash on their own.

chapters.title: Example: Rolling the fixed assets forward

scenes.head: Rolling the fixed assets forward

segs.say: At the end of 2027 Lantern’s property and equipment cost $120,000 with accumulated depreciation of $24,600. In 2028 it buys the second kitchen’s equipment ($60,000) and fit-out ($36,000) and Cold Brew’s fridges ($9,000), all in use from 1 April. Find 2028’s depreciation and the net book value at the end of 2028.

scenes.head: Rolling the fixed assets forward

segs.say: Step 2. New assets, nine months: kitchen equipment 60,000 ÷ 84 × 9 = 6,429; fit-out 36,000 ÷ 60 × 9 = 5,400; fridges 9,000 ÷ 60 × 9 = 1,350.
Step 3. Total depreciation: 35,979.

scenes.head: Rolling the fixed assets forward

segs.say: Depreciation $35,979; net property and equipment $164,421 at the end of 2028.

Depreciation nearly doubles from 2027’s $19,800, which is why 2028’s EBIT is negative though EBITDA is positive. The cash for the assets left in 2028; the cost reaches profit over the next five to seven years.

scenes.head: Lantern’s working capital schedule (fictional case; days are Ana’s assumptions)

segs.say: Lantern’s working capital schedule. Change the days in B4:B8: what happens to 2028’s cash need if invoiced customers take 40 days instead of 25? Then try paying suppliers faster (DPO 10): more cash is tied up. Pause the video and try it in the Explore section of this lesson.

scenes.head: Measuring receivables against all revenue

segs.say: Measuring receivables against all revenue. Café and online sales are paid by card on the day: they create no receivables. Measuring days against total revenue understates the days and misforecasts the balance when the mix changes.

scenes.head: Getting the sign of the change wrong

segs.say: Getting the sign of the change wrong. An increase in receivables or inventory uses cash; an increase in payables provides it. Subtract the change in operating working capital from profit, and check the sign against common sense.

scenes.head: Forgetting one-off balances

segs.say: Forgetting one-off balances. A large balance that will not recur (Lantern’s contract asset) must be run off explicitly, not grown with sales.

scenes.head: Depreciating from the start of the year

segs.say: Depreciating from the start of the year. An asset bought in April is used for nine months of that year. Depreciate from the month it comes into use, as the accounts do.

scenes.head: Capital spending far below depreciation

segs.say: Capital spending far below depreciation. A forecast that spends little on replacements lets the assets run down while margins stay high. Compare capex with depreciation and plan for assets reaching the end of their lives.

scenes.head: Putting cash and debt in working capital

segs.say: Putting cash and debt in working capital. Cash, the line of credit and the current portion of debt are financing, not operations. Keep them out of the operating working capital schedule, or the cash flow will count them twice.

scenes.head: Lenders to small businesses watch working capital closely because it is where cash disappears without anyone noticing.

segs.say: Lenders to small businesses watch working capital closely because it is where cash disappears without anyone noticing. A credit analyst will ask for the receivables ageing (who owes what, for how long) and compare the forecast days with the history. A forecast that improves collection from 25 days to 15 without a reason, such as new payment terms, is a red flag: it manufactures cash on paper.

scenes.head: In larger companies, capital spending is planned in a separate capital budget, project by project, and the model takes its totals.

segs.say: In larger companies, capital spending is planned in a separate capital budget, project by project, and the model takes its totals. Analysts covering listed companies compare capex with depreciation and with the company’s stated plans in its 10-K, and a gap between them is one of the first questions they ask management.

scenes.head: With the two schedules, Ana can see where 2028’s cash goes: $105,000 into the kitchen and fridges, offset by $15,219 released from working capital…

segs.say: With the two schedules, Ana can see where 2028’s cash goes: $105,000 into the kitchen and fridges, offset by $15,219 released from working capital and the depreciation added back to profit. What pays for the gap is the subject of the next lesson: the term loan, Hollis Avery’s money and the line of credit.

scenes.head: What to remember

segs.say: Operating working capital is the cash tied up in receivables, inventory and prepayments, less what suppliers, staff and customers have advanced; a rise uses cash and a fall releases it.
Forecast each balance as a flow times days ÷ 365, measured against the right flow: invoiced revenue for receivables, cost of goods for inventory and payables.
Run off one-off balances explicitly, and watch for one-off releases that flatter a year’s cash.
A fixed asset schedule lists each asset’s cost, start month, monthly depreciation and life; depreciation runs from the month an asset comes into use.
Roll property and equipment forward: opening net book value + capital spending − depreciation = closing.
Test capital spending against depreciation and asset lives; plan replacements and refits, which make real capex lumpy.
State the simplifications: book depreciation used for tax, leases kept at equal right-of-use asset and liability, the second kitchen’s rent expensed.
